works.title: EchoVision / Nocturnal Fugue
works.creators: Botao Amber Hu, Jiabao Li and collaborators
works.occasions: Fusebox 2024 under Congress Avenue Bridge; festival/gallery and IEEE VISAP circulation
works.publics: Passers-by, festival and gallery visitors, bat/conservation publics, technologists
works.summary:
*EchoVision* was directed by Botao Amber Hu and Jiabao Li with Xiaobo Aaron Hu, Jianan Johanna Liu, Danlin Huang, Yilan Tao and bat expert Merlin Tuttle among the publicly documented collaborators. The 2024 work combines a bat-shaped optical-see-through MR mask with the live audiovisual performance *Nocturnal Fugue*. The mask uses a phone, LiDAR and voice input to render a visual analogue of echolocation.

A participant holds or wears the bat-shaped device and uses vocal sound to generate a spatial response. The work amplifies an otherwise inaccessible acoustic relation and stages the visitor’s voice as an active probe. Its first documented public presentation took place beneath the Congress Avenue Bridge bat colony during Fusebox 2024 in Austin, followed by festival, gallery and research circulation. The site gave the translation an immediate ecological referent while the animal-like mask made the interface socially inviting and photographable.
works.publics_text: Encountered publics include bridge passers-by and festival visitors (**D/CR**), later gallery and visualisation audiences (**D**), and bat-conservation publics addressed through scientific collaboration (**D/RI**). Bats are represented rather than enrolled in the apparatus. Urban planners and conservation decision-makers are proposed downstream publics, but their involvement is not yet demonstrated.
works.rq1: The principal gaps are an umwelt gap (ultrasound is inaccessible), a reach gap (bat science and immersive media each attract specialist publics), and an action gap between a brief encounter and bat-sensitive behaviour or planning.
works.rq2: The work uses sensory substitution, self-generated sound, an inviting animal-form prop, spectacle, in-habitat placement and performance. It makes the visitor’s own body part of the translation rather than presenting a fixed visualisation.
works.rq3: Rendering echo as vision may reproduce ocularcentrism and imply more access to bat perception than the mapping can support. The approachable bat form can broaden participation but also sentimentalise the animal. Partnership and circulation are documented; attitude, behaviour and policy effects are not.
works.evaluation: A strong flagship for sensory translation and public invitation, but a weak action-outcome case.
works.configuration: Inaccessible ultrasound and distracted publics → voice-driven MR and in-situ spectacle → festival/passers-by public → documented exposure and creator-reported engagement → false-fidelity and action-evidence tension → disclose the mapping and add follow-up with conservation-relevant publics.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for authorship, interface and venue; moderate for reach; weak for lasting action. Sources: [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3680530.3695460) and [`portfolio/echovision.md`](../../portfolio/echovision.md).
works.format: MR mask plus live audiovisual performance
works.practice_label: Reality Design Lab · Hu, Huang & collaborators

short.rq1: Ultrasound and bat navigation remain inaccessible, while conservation communication is often specialist-bound.
short.rq2: Voice-triggered sensory substitution, animal-form prop, in-habitat premiere and spectacle.
short.rq3: Visualising echolocation may re-centre vision and imply access to a bat umwelt; reach is documented more strongly than behavioural change.

works.title: FeltSight
works.creators: Danlin Huang, Botao Amber Hu, Yifei Liu, Dong Zhang; advisors
works.occasions: SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 Art Papers, Hong Kong
works.publics: Conference/art publics, XR designers, accessibility/disability publics implicated
works.summary:
*FeltSight* was led by Danlin Huang, with Botao Amber Hu, Yifei Liu, Dong Zhang and advisors Takatoshi Yoshida and Rem RunGu Lin. The 2025 artwork draws on the star-nosed mole’s tactile navigation. It combines wearable haptic proximity gloves with a mixed-reality headset and deliberately reduced visual information.

Participants navigate a sparse point-cloud environment in which nearby objects become available through gesture and haptic response rather than continuous visual display. The design does not simply add touch to a visual scene. It withholds vision so that touch and bodily movement organise attention. This sensory reprioritisation makes the work an important counterpoint to projects that translate every nonhuman difference into images.
works.publics_text: The documented presentation is SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 Art Papers in Hong Kong (**D**). Encountered publics are therefore conference, immersive-art and technical audiences rather than an established general public. Accessibility and disability publics are implicated by the “near-blind” framing, although their participation or consultation is not documented (**RI**). The star-nosed mole is represented through analogy and no live animal is involved.
works.rq1: The work addresses an ocularcentric epistemic gap and the difficulty of making a tactile animal lifeworld compelling in a visually dominated venue. Its reach beyond an expert conference remains unknown.
works.rq2: Tactics include deliberate sensory deprivation, extended-range haptics, bodily navigation, gesture-triggered materialisation and a proposed open-source afterlife.
works.rq3: The same reduction of vision that disrupts ocularcentrism may imply equivalence among simulated non-vision, human blindness and a mole’s tactile umwelt. Without disabled collaborators or users in the record, the analogy risks appropriating disability as an experiential device. Repository availability is not evidence of reuse or more-than-human benefit.
works.evaluation: Conceptually valuable because it reprioritises touch; public reach and nonhuman consequence remain thin.
works.configuration: Visual dominance → reduced reality and haptic navigation → conference/art public → documented demonstration → false-fidelity and disability-representation tension → add access co-design and separate animal analogy from human disability claims.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong bibliographic evidence, moderate system evidence, no public-impact study. Sources: [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3757369.3767605) and [`portfolio/feltsight.md`](../../portfolio/feltsight.md).
works.practice_label: Reality Design Lab · Hu, Huang & collaborators

short.rq1: Tactile lifeworlds are subordinated to sight and the work is still conference-bound.
short.rq2: Vision suppression, proximity haptics, gesture-materialised point clouds and open-source release.
short.rq3: Approximating a near-blind animal through simulated non-vision risks both false fidelity and unexamined disability analogies.

works.title: FungiSync
works.creators: Botao Amber Hu, Danlin Huang, Yilan Tao, Xiaobo Hu, Rem Lin
works.occasions: SIGGRAPH 2025 Immersive Pavilion, Vancouver
works.publics: Immersive-art and research publics; fungal/ecological publics represented
works.summary:
*FungiSync* is credited to Botao Amber Hu, Danlin Huang, Yilan Elan Tao, Xiaobo Aaron Hu and Rem RunGu Lin in the publication record, with a project-page/paper credit discrepancy documented in the case file. The work dates from 2024 and was presented at the 2025 SIGGRAPH Immersive Pavilion.

Multiple participants wear HoloKit-style AR/MR devices and enter a synchronised, perspective-merging ritual. Rather than presenting mycorrhizae as a diagram, the work invites a group to experience distributed perception and coordinated action. Human co-presence becomes the expressive material through which a fungal-network relation is imagined.
works.publics_text: The verified public occasion is SIGGRAPH 2025 in Vancouver (**D**). Encountered publics are immersive-media visitors, artists and researchers. Fungal/ecological publics are represented, not directly involved. The installation’s group format produces a temporary participant public inside the encounter, but there is no evidence that this collectivity persists afterward.
works.rq1: The work addresses the invisibility of underground relations and the difficulty of communicating distributed, non-individual agency outside biology and posthuman theory.
works.rq2: It uses collective ritual, synchronised embodiment, perspective merging and shared-control aesthetics. The tactic shifts the unit of experience from an individual viewer to a temporary group.
works.rq3: Mycorrhizal relations are staged through human social coordination, which may turn a heterogeneous ecological network into a harmonious person-like subject. Spectacular togetherness can suppress competition, disturbance, scientific uncertainty and species specificity. Authorship discrepancies also show how collective technical labour can become unstable in public retelling.
works.evaluation: Useful as a relational-tactic case, but evidence of public interpretation or ecological action is absent.
works.configuration: Invisible distributed ecology → shared MR ritual → temporary participant collective → documented exhibition only → over-attribution and harmony bias → expose the analogy and retain conflict and uncertainty in interpretation.
works.evidence_boundary: Project mechanism and venue are documented; audience interpretation, fungal accuracy and action are unmeasured. Sources: [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3721245.3734040) and [`portfolio/fungisync.md`](../../portfolio/fungisync.md).
works.practice_label: Reality Design Lab · Hu, Huang & collaborators

short.rq1: Distributed fungal relations are invisible and difficult to narrate without turning a network into a person-like subject.
short.rq2: Perspective merging, synchronised collective movement and ritualised co-presence.
short.rq3: The designer scripts what counts as fungal collectivity; spectacular togetherness can displace ecological specificity and labour.

works.title: TentacUs
works.creators: Yiyang Sun, Ziying Chen, La Luo, Botao Amber Hu
works.occasions: SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 XR, Hong Kong
works.publics: XR/festival participants, design researchers, cephalopod publics represented
works.summary:
*TentacUs* was created by Yiyang Sun, Ziying Chen, La Luo and Botao Amber Hu. The 2025 XR work uses soft-textile gloves, embedded smartphones, tethering and shared-control interaction to explore octopus distributed cognition.

Participants form a ring and become mutually dependent limbs of a staged tentacular body. The group must coordinate movement through distributed signals rather than a single central controller. Tactile and, in the arXiv-described configuration, EMS cues redistribute agency across the assembled bodies. The project makes a conceptual claim about cognition perceptible through collective movement rather than explanatory text.
works.publics_text: The verified presentation is SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 XR in Hong Kong (**D**). The encountered public is primarily an XR/festival and research audience. Participants become performers for onlookers as well as users. Octopuses are neither present nor beneficiaries; cephalopod-science and animal-ethics publics are implicated through representation (**RI**).
works.rq1: Distributed cephalopod cognition is difficult to communicate and commonly reduced to the slogan of “nine brains.” The work also faces a conference-niche reach gap.
works.rq2: It uses physical tethering, shared control, group choreography, tactile redistribution and conspicuous collective performance. The social spectacle is part of the recruitment mechanism.
works.rq3: Human coordination is used as a proxy for octopus embodiment, and the work may overstate access to cephalopod experience. The participant ring makes distributed agency legible but can stabilise one disputed scientific story as an experiential truth. EMS also raises consent and accessibility questions for human participants.
works.evaluation: A vivid embodiment comparator, but not evidence of understanding or action for octopuses.
works.configuration: Abstract distributed cognition → tethered bodily collective → XR participant/observer public → documented presentation → biological exoticism and consent tension → state the analogy, scientific limits and bodily participation requirements.
works.evidence_boundary: Bibliographic and venue evidence are moderate; public response and action are absent. Sources: [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3761667.3761962) and [`portfolio/tentacus.md`](../../portfolio/tentacus.md).
works.format: tethered collective XR and soft-textile interfaces
works.practice_label: Reality Design Lab · Hu, Huang & collaborators

short.rq1: Cephalopod cognition is hard to communicate beyond specialist science and is easily reduced to the nine-brains trope.
short.rq2: Shared control, tethered bodies, tactile/EMS cues and group choreography.
short.rq3: Human bodies perform a curated model of octopus cognition; the work may turn biological difference into an exotic metaphor.

works.title: City of Sparkles
works.creators: Botao Hu, Yang Liu, Ran Duan
works.occasions: SIGGRAPH 2019; SIGGRAPH Asia and IEEE VR presentations in 2025
works.publics: Immersive-art, AI and computing publics
works.summary:
*City of Sparkles* was conceived by Botao Hu with interaction engineering by Yang Liu and composition by Ran Duan. The VR work premiered in 2019 and was re-created for newer immersive hardware in 2025. Its focal “other” is Zoe, an AI/artificial-life character moving through data landscapes.

Visitors enter a virtual city structured by geotagged sentiment and memory fragments. Zoe provides an approachable narrative figure through which machine perception and data life can be imagined. The later move from HTC Vive to Apple Vision Pro makes technological re-platforming itself part of the project’s afterlife.
works.publics_text: The work was presented at SIGGRAPH 2019 and returned in 2025 through SIGGRAPH Asia Art Papers and IEEE VR/VRW contexts (**D**). Its publics are immersive-art, computer-graphics and AI audiences. No ecological community or biological nonhuman is involved, so the project remains a scope-boundary case.
works.rq1: Artificial-life perception is abstract and difficult to discuss outside specialist AI and immersive-media venues. Hardware obsolescence adds a decay gap.
works.rq2: The work uses character familiarity, narrative worldbuilding, interactive spatial immersion, affective memory data and later re-platforming.
works.rq3: Treating AI as more-than-human may productively challenge a human/nonhuman binary, but it can also naturalise corporate data systems and divert ecological attention. Zoe’s personhood is entirely designed. Technological maintenance shows durability but not broader action.
works.evaluation: Valuable boundary case for scope and decay; keep analytically separate from biological cases.
works.configuration: Abstract machine perception and obsolescence → anthropomorphic VR narrative plus re-platforming → AI/immersive publics → repeated venue presence → scope expansion and corporate-infrastructure tension → retain as a labelled boundary case.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for bibliographic trajectory; no measured public consequence. Sources: [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3306449.3328815) and [`portfolio/city-of-sparkles.md`](../../portfolio/city-of-sparkles.md).
works.practice_label: Reality Design Lab · Hu, Huang & collaborators

short.rq1: Machine perception and data life are abstract, while the ecological scope of more-than-human design is contested.
short.rq2: Narrative character, memory fragments, immersive worldbuilding and cross-platform maintenance.
short.rq3: Anthropomorphising AI may naturalise corporate data systems as innocent life and expand the field away from ecological beings.

works.title: Being the Creek
works.creators: Yangyang Yang, Kimiko Ryokai
works.occasions: UC Berkeley creek-side pilot; CHI 2025
works.publics: Campus passers-by, study participants, watershed publics; Ohlone histories implicated
works.summary:
*Being the Creek* was led by Yangyang Yang with Kimiko Ryokai. It was developed around Strawberry Creek on the University of California, Berkeley campus, with a pilot publicly described in 2023 and a CHI publication in 2025.

Participants carry a tablet along the creek and must lie down at specific sites to unlock an AR journey through historical phases. Sound, smell, rock warmth and water coolness join first-person narration to interrupt upright, rapid campus movement. The work tries to make the creek noticeable as a historical and relational body rather than as scenery or drainage infrastructure.
works.publics_text: The primary context is an outdoor campus study/pilot (**D/CR**) rather than a gallery. Encountered publics include recruited participants and campus users; watershed stewards and university decision-makers are potential but undocumented publics. Ohlone histories and Indigenous relations are invoked, making Indigenous communities an affected/represented public even though co-creation is not documented.
works.rq1: The familiar creek is overlooked by daily passers-by, and its temporal, ecological and colonial histories exceed a brief encounter. A stewardship-action gap remains after perspective taking.
works.rq2: The work uses in-habitat placement, enforced bodily posture, first-person address, multisensory prompts and layered temporal narrative.
works.rq3: Speaking as the creek may overwrite otherness with human emotion. Requiring participants to lie down may exclude some bodies. Ohlone/animist framing without documented partnership raises appropriation and authority questions. Vivid pilot responses cannot be treated as evidence of later study outcomes.
works.evaluation: A strong situated noticing case with unresolved appropriation, access and stewardship outcomes.
works.configuration: Everyday campus invisibility → posture-gated multisensory AR → recruited campus public → pilot exposure/reflection → projection, access and Indigenous-authority tensions → add co-authorship, alternative postures and stewardship follow-up.
works.evidence_boundary: Publication existence is verified; some interaction detail remains creator/institution-reported. Sources: [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713713) and [`portfolio/being-the-creek.md`](../../portfolio/being-the-creek.md).

short.rq1: A familiar campus creek is passed daily without attention, and its long temporal history is difficult to encounter.
short.rq2: Lying-down posture, first-person narration, multisensory prompts and in-situ historical layering.
short.rq3: Speaking as the creek risks projection; Ohlone/animist framing and bodily accessibility require stronger co-authorship and access evidence.

works.title: Chthulucene
works.creators: Jiabao Li with choreographic, performance, media and illustration collaborators
works.occasions: Venice Architecture Biennale collateral exhibition; SIGGRAPH 2023; Exploratorium and other international venues
works.publics: Art, architecture and technology publics; cephalopods represented
works.summary:
*Chthulucene* was conceived and directed by Jiabao Li with producers, choreographers, performers, musicians, filmmakers, an octopus synthesist and illustrator credited on the official page. The project circulated from 2022 through at least 2024.

The work imagines humans approaching extinction while octopuses inherit a flooded world. Contact improvisation stages decentralised coordination; AI style transfer merges dancers and cephalopod imagery; speculative illustrations show posthuman archaeological and political scenes. The project’s concise premise allows it to move across live performance, video, exhibition, publication and conversation.
works.publics_text: Documented occasions include the Venice Architecture Biennale collateral programme in 2023, SIGGRAPH 2023 Art Gallery, Exploratorium, Currents New Media and other art/performance venues (**CR/D**). Publics include art, architecture, technology and speculative-design audiences. Cephalopods are represented; no live octopus participates. Scientific and conservation publics are invoked through collaborators and framing, but no downstream action is demonstrated.
works.rq1: Deep time, extinction and distributed cognition are difficult to narrate beyond specialist theory. The work also faces the problem of retaining qualification and collaborator labour as its premise travels.
works.rq2: It uses speculative fabulation, a one-sentence counterfactual, contact improvisation, AI image transformation, cross-media illustration and repeated international restaging.
works.rq3: Octopus cognition and extinction can become aesthetic resources for human self-reflection. A highly retellable story may simplify evolutionary science, treat species as symbols and obscure the many collaborators who produce the encounter. Circulation demonstrates reach and decay resistance, not action.
works.evaluation: Highly retellable and politically generative, but action and cephalopod benefit are not evidenced.
works.configuration: Abstract extinction/deep time → compact speculative story and multi-format performance → international cultural publics → documented restaging → charisma, scientific-fidelity and labour-erasure tensions → preserve credits and counter-readings with every retelling.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for creator credits and exhibition list; no audience or ecological outcome evidence. Sources: [official project page](https://www.jiabaoli.org/chthulucene), [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3588428.3593823) and [`portfolio/chthulucene.md`](../../portfolio/chthulucene.md).
works.format: performance, AI imagery and speculative illustration

short.rq1: Deep-time extinction and distributed intelligence are difficult to make retellable outside art and theory niches.
short.rq2: Speculative worldbuilding, contact improvisation, AI style transfer and repeated international exhibition.
short.rq3: Octopus cognition and extinction become aesthetic resources; collaborator labour and scientific qualification can disappear as the premise travels.

works.title: Carbon Farm
works.creators: Jiabao Li, Ben Evanson and technical/scientific collaborators
works.occasions: SIGGRAPH Asia 2024 and international art/design presentations
works.publics: Gallery/festival visitors, diners/participants, climate and biodesign publics
works.summary:
*Carbon Farm* is credited to Jiabao Li and Ben J. Evanson with a wider engineering, biomaterial and scientific team. Public iterations span 2023–2025, with a SIGGRAPH Asia publication in 2024.

Participants contribute breath or speech. The installation captures CO2, displays the process and routes carbon into living algae cultures; the project page further describes harvested algae becoming food and bioplastic. Objects, badges and a dining performance extend the installation into a material narrative about metabolic participation. The work therefore goes beyond representing carbon and installs a breath-to-culture-to-output pathway.
works.publics_text: Presentations include SIGGRAPH Asia 2024 and international art, design and symposium settings listed by the creators (**D/CR**). Encountered publics are gallery/festival visitors and dining participants. Climate, carbon-removal and biodesign publics are addressed. Algae are materially enrolled and require ongoing care; engineers, culture maintainers and venue staff are participating publics whose labour should remain visible.
works.rq1: Atmospheric carbon and algal metabolism are invisible, while climate responsibility is typically encountered as remote statistics or expert infrastructure. A scale gap separates gallery materialisation from climate consequence.
works.rq2: Tactics include bodily contribution, real-time display, living culture, material transformation, participatory dining and portable objects that can carry the story.
works.rq3: The installation may individualise structural emissions and frame removal as a personal metabolic act. Algae can be instrumentalised as climate media; chemical, energy and maintenance inputs remain outside the most memorable story. The household version is proposed rather than adopted at scale.
works.evaluation: A rich material-action pathway, but not proof of climate mitigation or scalable adoption.
works.configuration: Abstract carbon cycle → breath-linked living-media pathway → gallery/dining climate public → documented participation and outputs → individualisation, lifecycle and microbial-care tensions → publish full lifecycle and maintenance evidence.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for public project facts; climate efficacy, product adoption and ecological benefit are unverified. Sources: [official project page](https://www.jiabaoli.org/carbon-farm), [ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3680529.3688967) and [`portfolio/carbon-farm.md`](../../portfolio/carbon-farm.md).
works.format: living-media carbon-capture installation and dining performance

short.rq1: Carbon metabolism is invisible and climate responsibility is usually presented at an abstract planetary scale.
short.rq2: Breath capture, real-time CO2 display, algae culture, bioplastic/food outputs and participatory ritual.
short.rq3: The work can individualise structural emissions and instrumentalise algae; lifecycle inputs and household feasibility are not independently established.

works.title: In the Eyes of the Animal
works.creators: Marshmallow Laser Feast
works.occasions: Grizedale Forest; Sundance 2016; international festivals/galleries
works.publics: Forest visitors, ticketed festival/gallery publics, immersive-media publics
works.summary:
*In the Eyes of the Animal* was created by Marshmallow Laser Feast, publicly identified with directors Barnaby Steel, Ersin Han Ersin and Robin McNicholas. The work began in 2015 and toured for several years.

Visitors enter a VR/XR forest constructed from LiDAR and drone capture, 360-degree imagery, binaural audio, haptics and scent. The experience moves through stylised perceptual positions associated with woodland beings including mosquito, dragonfly, frog and owl. Its first forest siting connected the simulation to a material woodland, while later festival and gallery versions increased accessibility and circulation.
works.publics_text: The work premiered at Grizedale Forest and appeared at Sundance in 2016, followed by international immersive-art and gallery touring (**D/CR**). Encountered publics include forest visitors and ticketed festival/museum audiences. Wildlife and ecological publics are represented; animals are not participants or documented beneficiaries. High production costs and venue infrastructure shape who can encounter it.
works.rq1: The work tackles the impossibility of directly occupying another species’ umwelt and the difficulty of attracting non-specialists to perceptual ecology.
works.rq2: It combines sensory substitution, spectacle, animal-perspective sequencing, in-habitat placement, haptics and scent. Touring creates a multi-year cultural afterlife.
works.rq3: Multisensory intensity can be mistaken for scientific fidelity. The experience privileges a human visitor’s sublime transformation and may aestheticise animal difference. Broad circulation and awards do not establish wildlife action, habitat support or durable attitude change.
works.evaluation: An influential reach and immersion exemplar; no demonstrated wildlife action or durable attitude change.
works.configuration: Inaccessible animal umwelten → blockbuster multisensory translation → forest/festival/museum publics → documented touring → false-fidelity, access and spectacle tensions → disclose speculative mappings and evaluate post-visit consequences.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for work form and touring, no formal impact evidence. Sources: [creator project page](https://marshmallowlaserfeast.com/project/in-the-eyes-of-the-animal/) and [`portfolio/in-the-eyes-of-the-animal.md`](../../portfolio/in-the-eyes-of-the-animal.md).

short.rq1: Animal umwelten are inaccessible and nature interpretation often remains didactic or specialist.
short.rq2: LiDAR, 360 imagery, binaural audio, haptics, scent, forest siting and festival touring.
short.rq3: Sensory translation can imply impossible fidelity and turn species difference into premium spectacle.

works.title: Pollinator Pathmaker
works.creators: Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg with horticulturalists, pollinator experts and commissioning partners
works.occasions: Eden Project; Serpentine; Berlin edition; distributed online planting
works.publics: Garden visitors, online planters, cultural publics, gardeners; pollinators as intended beneficiaries
works.summary:
*Pollinator Pathmaker* was initiated by Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg with horticulturalists, pollinator specialists, commissioning institutions and Google Arts & Culture. It began with the Eden Project commission in 2021 and continues through institutional and public-generated editions.

An algorithm generates planting schemes based on pollinator needs rather than conventional human aesthetics. Public gardens become living sculptures, and a web tool allows people to create local planting plans. A “pollinator vision” mode shifts the visual frame, but the project’s strongest tactic is material: a participant can plant habitat rather than only simulate insect perception.
works.publics_text: Documented editions include the Eden Project in Cornwall, the Serpentine in London and a Berlin edition, alongside distributed public use of the online tool (**D/CR**). Encountered publics include garden visitors, art audiences, gardeners and online users. Participating publics plant and maintain editions. Pollinators are the intended beneficiaries and material users, while horticultural experts act as proxies. Local land managers and institutions are decision-capable publics.
works.rq1: Pollinators are overlooked, and planting systems usually prioritise human beauty. The project also addresses the action gap by providing an implementable pathway beyond awareness.
works.rq2: Tactics include designing for nonhuman preference, algorithmic planning, living seasonal material, public propagation, a web tool and alternative visualisation.
works.rq3: Algorithms and experts decide how insect preference becomes legible. Planting is a stronger action pathway than most portfolio encounters, but garden creation alone does not prove pollinator use, survival or population benefit. Access depends on land, time and maintenance capacity.
works.evaluation: One of the strongest cases because the work is for nonhumans and creates habitat, while outcome evidence remains incomplete.
works.configuration: Human-centred planting and pollinator invisibility → algorithmic habitat design and distributed planting → garden visitors/planters plus pollinators → documented gardens and tool access → proxy, land-access and ecological-outcome tensions → pair participation records with ecological monitoring.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for commissions, planting pathway and public tool; ecological outcomes remain incomplete. Sources: [Serpentine project page](https://www.serpentinegalleries.org/whats-on/alexandra-daisy-ginsberg-pollinator-pathmaker/) and [`portfolio/pollinator-pathmaker.md`](../../portfolio/pollinator-pathmaker.md).
works.format: algorithmic living garden plus public web tool

short.rq1: Pollinators are overlooked and planting is usually optimised for human beauty.
short.rq2: Algorithmic species-oriented planting, pollinator-vision interface, living seasonal habitat and distributed public editions.
short.rq3: Experts and algorithms proxy insect preference; ecological benefit must be measured rather than inferred from planting.

works.title: Amphibious Architecture
works.creators: The Living, Chris Woebken, Natalie Jeremijenko’s Environmental Health Clinic
works.occasions: East and Bronx Rivers; Toward the Sentient City
works.publics: Waterfront passers-by, exhibition visitors, SMS participants, civic/environmental publics
works.summary:
*Amphibious Architecture* was created in 2009 by The Living (David Benjamin and Soo-in Yang), Chris Woebken and Natalie Jeremijenko’s Environmental Health Clinic.

Floating tubes in the East and Bronx Rivers sensed fish presence and dissolved oxygen. LEDs made activity visible at the water surface, while a two-way SMS system allowed people to “text” the river and receive responses. The installation combined instrument-grounded environmental sensing with a deliberately personified conversational layer.
works.publics_text: The work was installed in New York waterways in connection with *Toward the Sentient City* and ran through the end of 2009 (**D**). Publics included waterfront passers-by, exhibition visitors and SMS users. Fish and aquatic systems were sensed, while local residents, water managers and civic organisations were issue or decision-capable publics. There is little evidence that these latter publics took consequential action.
works.rq1: Aquatic life and water quality are physically close yet perceptually hidden. Civic sensing also faces an afterlife gap when temporary infrastructure is removed.
works.rq2: The project uses live environmental sensing, light translation, public siting, SMS access and personification to turn a waterway into an addressable interlocutor.
works.rq3: The river’s “voice” is authored through designers and software. Conversational accessibility can simplify ecological uncertainty and suggest reciprocity where only data retrieval occurs. Temporary deployment and weak outcome records limit claims about stewardship or governance.
works.evaluation: Historically important for public environmental interfaces and a useful negative decay case.
works.configuration: Hidden urban aquatic life → live sensing and textable river → waterfront/SMS public → documented temporary interaction → ventriloquism and weak-decay tensions → publish mapping, civic follow-up and maintenance history.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong project documentation; weak action and durability evidence. Sources: [Expanded Environment project page](https://expandedenvironment.org/amphibiousarchitecture/) and [`portfolio/amphibious-architecture.md`](../../portfolio/amphibious-architecture.md).
works.format: floating sensors, LEDs and public SMS

short.rq1: Urban aquatic life and dissolved oxygen are invisible to waterfront publics.
short.rq2: Real-time civic sensing, light translation, two-way SMS and waterway personification.
short.rq3: A human-authored river voice may simplify ecology; a temporary installation offers little evidence of governance or maintenance.

works.title: Skotopoiesis
works.creators: Špela Petrič
works.occasions: Gallery/live performance settings
works.publics: Small gallery audience, performance-art publics; cress materially affected
works.summary:
*Skotopoiesis* is a 2015 durational performance by Špela Petrič involving a field of germinating cress and the artist’s body.

Petrič stands for approximately twelve hours so that her shadow deprives part of the cress of light. The plants bend and etiolate, while the performer’s body also undergoes fatigue and compression. No digital interface or explanatory spectacle mediates the relation. The encounter is slow, materially reciprocal in effect and intentionally resistant to rapid public consumption.
works.publics_text: The work was presented as a live gallery/performance encounter (**D/CR**). Its encountered public is small and time-dependent. Performance and bioart audiences witness the relation, while the cress is materially altered. The project does not target mass circulation and offers limited participation beyond witnessing.
works.rq1: Vegetal time and phototropic response are difficult to notice within ordinary gallery rhythms. The work turns limited scale into a deliberate method rather than a failure.
works.rq2: Tactics include durational co-presence, bodily endurance, shadow, plant growth, withholding of technological mediation and anti-spectacle.
works.rq3: Intimacy resists attention-economy demands but restricts access. The artist remains the author of the conditions and intentionally changes plant development. Calling the relation reciprocal should not erase asymmetry in who initiates, can leave and receives cultural credit.
works.evaluation: A powerful counterexample showing that effective noticing need not mean scale or technology.
works.configuration: Slow plant response and gallery distraction → twelve-hour bodily shadowing → small witnessing public → direct material trace → access, control and authorship asymmetry → preserve slowness while documenting plant treatment and alternative access.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for form and intention, no broader public/action study. Sources: [artist project page](https://www.spelapetric.org/scotopoiesis) and [`portfolio/skotopoiesis.md`](../../portfolio/skotopoiesis.md).

short.rq1: Vegetal time and growth are hard to notice within rapid gallery attention.
short.rq2: Human shadow, bodily endurance, plant phototropism and deliberate anti-spectacle.
short.rq3: The artist intentionally alters plant growth and still controls the conditions; intimacy limits access but resists attention-economy demands.

works.title: PigeonBlog
works.creators: Beatriz da Costa with engineers, students and pigeon fanciers
works.entity: Homing pigeons and urban air pollution
works.occasions: ISEA 2006, San Jose; public flights and online interface
works.publics: Environmental-justice publics, festival/online viewers, pigeon-fancier collaborators; pigeons as participants
works.summary:
*PigeonBlog* was led by Beatriz da Costa with engineers, students and pigeon fanciers. It operated from 2006 to 2008 and used homing pigeons as mobile air-quality sensing participants.

Pigeons carried custom lightweight sensor backpacks that streamed geolocated pollution data to a live online map. Public flights combined citizen sensing, tactical media and the figure of the “civilian pigeon journalist.” The work made pollution visible while intentionally unsettling the authority of official environmental monitoring.
works.publics_text: Public flights were associated with ISEA 2006 in San Jose and online circulation (**D**). Participating publics included students, engineers and pigeon fanciers; encountered publics included festival and online viewers. Environmental-justice communities were an issue public addressed by the pollution framing. Pigeons were live participants and bore the equipment, making welfare and training expertise central rather than peripheral.
works.rq1: Pollution is ambient and unevenly distributed, while official sensing is expert-controlled. Public attention to exposure rarely persists after a media event.
works.rq2: Tactics include animal-borne sensing, live data, public flight, activist naming, low-cost technical making and web circulation.
works.rq3: The project redistributed sensing authority but enrolled pigeons as labourers. The journalist metaphor grants symbolic agency while humans control routes, devices and interpretation. Technical and activist value therefore coexists with welfare and consent concerns. The project’s short life also limits institutional durability.
works.evaluation: A canonical activist case whose ethical controversy is analytically indispensable.
works.configuration: Invisible unequal pollution → pigeon-borne live sensing → festival/online environmental-justice public → documented flights/data → animal-labour and welfare tension → retain tactical critique while foregrounding ACI governance and aftercare.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong historical project evidence; limited downstream policy evidence. Sources: [Radical Data documentation](https://radicaldata.org/projects/pigeonblog/) and [`portfolio/pigeonblog.md`](../../portfolio/pigeonblog.md).
works.format: wearable sensing, public flights and live web map

short.rq1: Pollution exposure and environmental injustice are difficult to perceive at street level.
short.rq2: Pigeon-borne sensors, geolocation, live data, activist framing and public performance.
short.rq3: Pigeons become sensing labourers; civic visibility competes with welfare, consent and data-quality questions.

works.title: Urban Forest Visual / Email a Tree
works.creators: City of Melbourne Urban Forest and Ecology Team
works.medium: Web map; tree IDs and email addresses
works.occasions: Melbourne municipal platform; global press/social circulation
works.publics: Residents, correspondents, municipal staff, urban-forestry publics; street trees represented
works.summary:
Melbourne’s Urban Forest and Ecology Team launched the municipal Urban Forest Visual in 2013. Individual street trees received IDs and email addresses through a public map.

The system was intended to support reporting about tree condition, but people began writing personal messages to trees. Municipal staff sometimes replied in the tree’s voice. A functional infrastructure therefore became an affective correspondence platform, making individual trees addressable and memorable without requiring specialist ecological knowledge.
works.publics_text: This is a municipal web service rather than a gallery work. Encountered publics include residents and global correspondents reached through press and social circulation (**D/secondary**). Participating publics include staff who maintain records and write replies. Urban foresters and city officials are decision-capable publics. Street trees are represented and managed; they do not author the correspondence.
works.rq1: Urban trees are infrastructural background and difficult to recognise as individuals. Municipal datasets are usually inaccessible or emotionally thin.
works.rq2: Tactics include individual naming/address, a low-threshold web map, direct correspondence, humour and personified response.
works.rq3: Human-written replies ventriloquise trees and can turn civic ecology into charm. Charismatic correspondence may privilege some trees while canopy inequity, maintenance budgets and removals remain less visible. Message counts demonstrate participation, not stewardship outcomes.
works.evaluation: Excellent reach and relational-access comparator; weak evidence of lasting stewardship.
works.configuration: Anonymous urban infrastructure → addressable tree email → resident/global correspondence public → documented messages → ventriloquism and charisma/canopy-justice tension → link affective exchange to transparent municipal care records.
works.evidence_boundary: Municipal/project facts are supported mainly by institutional and reputable secondary documentation; later impact is unclear. Sources: [Smithsonian account](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/when-you-give-tree-email-address-180955851/) and [`portfolio/email-a-tree.md`](../../portfolio/email-a-tree.md).
works.format: municipal map, IDs and email addresses

short.rq1: Street trees are infrastructural background and difficult to address as individuals.
short.rq2: Individual addresses, personified correspondence, municipal interface and low-threshold participation.
short.rq3: Replies written by staff ventriloquise trees; charismatic messages can outrun maintenance data and equitable canopy politics.

works.title: Environmental Health Clinic / xClinic
works.creators: Natalie Jeremijenko
works.entity: Urban environmental systems and animal proxies
works.occasions: NYU/public consultations and associated interventions
works.publics: “Impatients,” local residents, students, civic/environmental actors; animals and habitats affected
works.summary:
Natalie Jeremijenko’s Environmental Health Clinic emerged at New York University around 2007–2009. It treats people as “impatients” and offers prescriptions for environmental action rather than medical diagnoses.

Participants bring an environmental concern and receive a tailored action, experiment or design intervention. The clinic format reworks professional authority: environmental problems become conditions requiring collective, situated action rather than expert information alone. Related prescriptions have involved air, water, food systems and animal proxies.
works.publics_text: The project operated through public consultations, university infrastructure and associated urban interventions (**D/secondary**). Participating publics include individual impatients, students and collaborators. Affected publics include neighbourhood residents, urban animals and environments. Civic agencies and professional organisations are potential decision-capable publics, but systematic evidence of adoption is sparse.
works.rq1: Environmental knowledge is often separated from everyday agency. The clinic addresses an action gap but trades broad reach for bespoke depth and faces a follow-through problem.
works.rq2: Tactics include institutional parody, one-to-one consultation, behavioural/design prescriptions, public experiment and reframing concern as an actionable condition.
works.rq3: The clinician role can reproduce expert authority even while critiquing it. Live animals used as sensors or proxies may be instrumentalised. The anti-scale model may enable specificity but leave unequal access and long-term maintenance unresolved.
works.evaluation: Important activist-service model, but needs better primary archival and outcome evidence.
works.configuration: Expertised environmental concern → participatory clinic and prescription → local participant/issue public → documented consultations, weak longitudinal trace → authority, animal-proxy and anti-scale tensions → record adherence, outcomes and affected-community governance.
works.evidence_boundary: Historically significant but primary archive and outcome evidence are weaker than for most core cases. Sources: [`portfolio/environmental-health-clinic.md`](../../portfolio/environmental-health-clinic.md) and its linked reference record.
works.entity_short: urban environmental systems and animal proxies

short.rq1: Environmental problems appear as expert diagnoses rather than relations people can act within.
short.rq2: One-to-one consultations, prescriptions, local experiments and anti-institutional clinic framing.
short.rq3: The model is intentionally hard to scale; animal proxies and expert authority remain, and follow-through is poorly documented.

works.title: Feral Robotic Dogs
works.creators: Natalie Jeremijenko with Bronx teens and William Kavesh
works.occasions: Bronx River; later public releases in Orlando, New Haven and Boise
works.publics: Youth co-makers, local residents, environmental-justice and maker publics
works.summary:
*Feral Robotic Dogs* was initiated by Natalie Jeremijenko in the early 2000s and developed through community workshops in which commercially available robotic toy dogs were repurposed as environmental sensing devices. A frequently documented 2003 iteration involved Bronx teenagers, community collaborators and roboticist William Kavesh.

Participants modified discarded or inexpensive toy dogs so that they could move through contaminated sites carrying sensors. Their apparently playful roaming converted invisible chemical exposure into a public, embodied search. The “feral” framing joined do-it-yourself engineering with environmental-justice inquiry: a consumer object designed for scripted obedience became a collectively reprogrammable field instrument.
works.publics_text: Workshops and public releases took place in the Bronx and were subsequently adapted in locations including New Haven, Orlando and Boise (**D/secondary**). Participating publics included young makers, educators, engineers and local environmental advocates. Residents near contaminated land formed an affected and issue public; environmental agencies and land managers were the relevant decision-capable publics. The robotic dogs are expressive proxies, not living more-than-human participants.
works.rq1: Toxic exposure is materially consequential yet visually absent, while credible measurement is commonly controlled by experts and agencies. Community members may therefore experience pollution without possessing public proof or a compelling means of displaying it.
works.rq2: The project uses low-cost hacking, zoomorphic movement, public workshops, collective field release and live sensing. Familiar toy behaviour lowers the threshold for approaching a technical and politically charged problem.
works.rq3: Play can redistribute technical confidence, but it can also make chronic contamination look like a temporary spectacle. Sensor accuracy, calibration and evidentiary status determine whether community-generated data can contest official accounts. The project also raises a representational tension: animal-like behaviour attracts attention even though no animal perspective is present.
works.evaluation: A strong tactical case for accessible activist sensing with modest evidence of downstream action.
works.configuration: Invisible and expert-controlled contamination → community-built roaming sensor → youth/resident environmental-justice public → documented workshops and releases → playful proxy, data-validity and institutional-recognition tensions → pair public sensing with calibration records, community ownership and an agency-facing pathway.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong historical evidence for the workshop method and public performances; weaker evidence for regulatory uptake or durable remediation. Sources: [Yale School of the Environment project account](https://environment.yale.edu/news/article/natalie-jeremijenko-feral-robotic-dogs) and [`portfolio/feral-robotic-dogs.md`](../../portfolio/feral-robotic-dogs.md).

sources.label: Yale School of the Environment project account

works.format: hacked toy robots and public release events

short.rq1: Contaminated land is unseen and environmental monitoring appears expensive and expert-owned.
short.rq2: Low-cost hacking, zoomorphic movement, participatory release and explicit low-fidelity sensing.
short.rq3: Playful dogs can overshadow community exposure and policy; crude sensors trade precision for legibility.

works.title: TreeWatch.net
works.creators: Kathy Steppe, Jonas von der Crone, Dirk De Pauw
works.occasions: Experimental forests, parks/schoolyards and online network
works.publics: Scientists, students, online followers, urban-tree publics; instrumented trees
works.summary:
*TreeWatch.net* is an ongoing tree-monitoring and public-communication network associated with Kathy Steppe and collaborators at Ghent University. The network became publicly visible in the mid-2010s and connects instrumented trees across research and public sites.

Sap-flow sensors, dendrometers and local weather instruments register otherwise imperceptible changes in water transport, growth and stress. Selected measurements are translated into web updates and first-person social-media posts. A tree thereby appears to report heat, drought, recovery or daily rhythms, while the scientific measurements remain available as the basis for the communication.
works.publics_text: The project operates through instrumented forests, parks and school or university sites, with a distributed online presence rather than a single exhibition (**D**). Scientists and technicians are participating publics; students, teachers, park visitors and online followers are encountered publics. Forestry and municipal land-management organisations are potentially decision-capable. Living trees are sensed participants, although humans determine what is measured and said.
works.rq1: Tree physiology unfolds internally and at temporal scales that do not align with casual observation. Specialist data can remain inaccessible even when it directly concerns public experiences of heat and drought.
works.rq2: Tactics include long-duration sensing, scientific visualisation, first-person personification, social distribution and emplacement in familiar public landscapes.
works.rq3: The first-person voice makes data legible but can imply intentional speech. Sensor selection privileges measurable processes and platform algorithms influence who encounters the posts. Following or liking a tree is evidence of attention, not of altered forestry practice or climate action.
works.evaluation: A stronger epistemic bridge than pure role-play, but public action and platform afterlife are uncertain.
works.configuration: Hidden physiological change → continuous sensing plus tree-authored social voice → scientific, educational and online publics → documented measurements and circulation → ventriloquism, metric/platform and action-gap tensions → keep the translation chain visible and connect alerts to care decisions.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for instrumentation and communication design; uneven for public interpretation, behavioural consequence and institutional adoption. Sources: [TreeWatch.net](https://treewatch.net/) and [`portfolio/treewatch.md`](../../portfolio/treewatch.md).

image.credit: Steppe et al., Frontiers in Plant Science 2016 (Figure 1)

short.rq1: Tree hydraulics and carbon exchange are scientifically legible but publicly remote.
short.rq2: Sap-flow and dendrometer data, real-time modelling and personified posts.
short.rq3: Instrument-grounded signals still require human-authored interpretation; platform dependence threatens continuity.

works.title: The Art of Listening: Under Water
works.creators: Jana Winderen with Tony Myatt
works.occasions: Art Basel Miami Beach 2019; Lenfest Center, Columbia 2022
works.publics: Art-fair/gallery listeners, sound-art and marine-ecology publics
works.summary:
*Art Listening Under Water* is a spatial sound installation by Jana Winderen with sound designer Tony Myatt. It was presented in 2019 in connection with Art Basel Miami Beach and later at the Lenfest Center for the Arts in New York in 2022.

Hydrophone recordings place listeners inside an acoustic field of underwater animals, ice, currents and human-generated noise. Rather than turning the recordings into a visual dashboard, the work preserves sound as sound and redistributes the audible range through a carefully composed loudspeaker environment. It asks audiences to encounter an inhabited ocean that ordinary human listening and land-based attention exclude.
works.publics_text: Documented presentations include Miami Beach in 2019 and Columbia University’s Lenfest Center in 2022 (**D**). Encountered publics include contemporary-art, sound-art, university and marine-environment audiences. The animals and habitats are recorded rather than present. Marine researchers and conservation organisations are interpretive allies, while shipping, fisheries and regulators are relevant but not demonstrably reached decision-capable publics.
works.rq1: Underwater life is physically remote and often drowned out in public discourse by visual representations. Anthropogenic noise is also difficult to perceive from land.
works.rq2: The work uses hydrophone field recording, spatial composition, low-frequency embodiment, darkness and within-modal amplification. It does not pretend to translate sound into a humanlike language.
works.rq3: Composition necessarily selects locations, species and intensities. Aesthetic immersion can make ecological disturbance affectively present, but it can also detach recordings from the infrastructures and jurisdictions producing the noise. Ticketed art access and the absence of an action pathway constrain political reach.
works.evaluation: Excellent non-visual translation; weak evidence of action beyond listening.
works.configuration: Inaudible and remote underwater relations → hydrophone recording and spatial audition → gallery/university listening public → documented presentations, interpretation outcomes unknown → compositional authority, aestheticisation and access tensions → retain acoustic specificity while naming sites, causes and response routes.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for authorship, medium and presentation; limited for audience research or conservation consequences. Sources: [Jana Winderen’s project documentation](https://www.janawinderen.com/exhibitions/the-art-of-listening-under-water) and [`portfolio/art-of-listening-under-water.md`](../../portfolio/art-of-listening-under-water.md).

short.rq1: Underwater acoustic ecologies and human noise are normally inaudible to land-based publics.
short.rq2: Hydrophone field recording, sound-to-sound amplification, spatial audio and gallery restaging.
short.rq3: Aesthetic immersion may beautify crisis and edit whole ecosystems into an authored composition.

works.title: The Sound of Light in Trees
works.creators: David Dunn
works.occasions: Field recording; album/CD and online circulation
works.publics: Sound-art listeners, forest scientists/managers, affected forest communities
works.summary:
*The Sound of Light in Trees* is a sound work by David Dunn, first published in 2006 and subsequently reissued. It emerged from field recordings of bark beetles and other organisms made with custom microphones and probes placed in or against trees.

Dunn’s recordings reveal clicks, pulses and granular textures produced inside bark and wood. The album makes a sub-bark acoustic world available to listeners who would otherwise encounter a forest mainly at human scale. Its title also destabilises sensory categories: what appears visually as light, tree and landscape becomes an internally active acoustic habitat.
works.publics_text: The work has circulated through recordings, radio, talks and sound-art contexts rather than a single stable exhibition (**D/secondary**). Encountered publics include experimental-music listeners, acoustic ecologists, entomologists and forest researchers. Forest managers form a possible decision-capable public. Bark beetles and trees are recorded participants but have no role in the later framing or circulation.
works.rq1: Life beneath bark is spatially concealed and temporally difficult to follow. Public accounts of bark beetles often reduce them to a visible outbreak or threat after complex interactions are already under way.
works.rq2: Tactics include probe-microphone invention, patient field listening, minimally recognisable acoustic composition and album-based circulation beyond the recording site.
works.rq3: Amplification can complicate the image of a silent tree, but interpretation can still fold beetles into a threat narrative. The recording apparatus and the composer determine what counts as signal. Claims that listening changes forestry intervention require evidence beyond the artwork’s documented circulation.
works.evaluation: A durable sonic artifact and strong epistemic case, with unresolved activist causality.
works.configuration: Concealed sub-bark life → custom contact/probe recording → sound-art and forest-science publics → durable recording archive → selection, pest-framing and action-gap tensions → contextualise species relations and distinguish auditory discovery from management impact.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for the recording work and its scientific-artistic method; limited for public-response and management outcomes. Sources: [artist release documentation](https://daviddunn.bandcamp.com/album/the-sound-of-light-in-trees) and [`portfolio/sound-of-light-in-trees.md`](../../portfolio/sound-of-light-in-trees.md).

short.rq1: Sub-bark insect activity is inaccessible even when it transforms whole forests.
short.rq2: Probe microphones, within-modal amplification, album circulation and field-science collaboration.
short.rq3: Recording can frame beetles primarily as threats; claimed management consequences are creator-reported and need independent evidence.

works.title: The Hive
works.creators: Wolfgang Buttress, BDP, Simmonds Studio, Stage One, BE Collective
works.occasions: UK Pavilion, Expo Milano 2015; Royal Botanic Gardens Kew
works.publics: Expo and botanic-garden visitors, design/media publics, beekeepers; managed colony
works.summary:
*The Hive* is an immersive architectural installation commissioned as the United Kingdom Pavilion for Expo Milano 2015. It was designed by Wolfgang Buttress with BDP, Simmonds Studio, Stage One and a wider scientific and production team, and was reconstructed at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, in 2016.

A lattice structure resembling a vast swarm surrounds visitors with light and sound. Signals from a living honeybee colony modulate the installation, creating a remote coupling between colony activity and the public environment. The project combines architecture, telemetry and spectacle to make collective insect life perceptible at human scale.
works.publics_text: The work was encountered by international-expo visitors in Milan and later by garden, family, tourist and educational publics at Kew (**D/CR**). Beekeepers, scientists, engineers and garden staff are participating and maintenance publics. A live colony supplies data but is geographically separate from visitors. Agricultural and biodiversity institutions are relevant decision-capable publics; reach to them should not be assumed from visitor volume.
works.rq1: Colony processes are spatially hidden, distributed across thousands of bees and difficult to apprehend through an individual-animal frame. Specialist monitoring alone does not make those processes publicly meaningful.
works.rq2: Tactics include monumental architecture, live telemetry, responsive LEDs, sound composition, biomimetic form, family-accessible immersion and reinstallation at a major public garden.
works.rq3: Spectacle delivers reach but may turn colony complexity into ambience. Honeybees’ cultural charisma can eclipse wild pollinator diversity and agricultural politics. Visitor numbers show exposure, not interpretation or changed practice. Continuous data and a rebuilt pavilion also depend on substantial technical and care labour.
works.evaluation: An exceptional reach/decay case, but not evidence of pollinator benefit.
works.configuration: Hidden collective insect activity → live-data architectural spectacle → expo and botanic-garden publics → very high documented exposure, thinner engagement evidence → charisma, spectacle and maintenance tensions → pair sensory scale with pollinator plurality and evaluated action pathways.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for commissioning, technical form and public presentation; weaker for what visitors learned or did afterwards. Sources: [Stage One project documentation](https://www.stageone.co.uk/projects/the-hive/) and [`portfolio/the-hive.md`](../../portfolio/the-hive.md).
works.format: architectural pavilion driven by live hive vibration

short.rq1: Bee-colony activity is hidden and pollinator discourse rarely reaches mass cultural venues.
short.rq2: Live accelerometer feed, LEDs, soundscape, architectural spectacle and permanent reinstallation.
short.rq3: Bee charisma, ticketing and monumental authorship can hide managed-colony welfare and team labour; footfall is not engagement.

works.title: Nukabot
works.creators: Dominique Chen and Ferment Media Research collaborators
works.occasions: Triennale di Milano; 2121 DESIGN SIGHT; Miraikan; other design venues
works.publics: Museum/design visitors, fermentation practitioners, cultural publics; microbial community
works.summary:
*Nukabot* is a family of fermented-food interfaces developed from 2019 onward by Dominique Chen and Ferment Media Research collaborators. Credits vary by iteration: the 2021 publication includes Chen, Young ah Seong, Hiraku Ogura, Yuto Mitani, Naoto Sekiya and Kiichi Moriya; the 2024 publication includes Chen, Youngah Seong and Kazuhiro Jo. Its central artefact is a sensor-equipped rice-bran fermentation vessel that communicates conditions relevant to microbial care.

Japanese nukadoko fermentation requires repeated mixing, smelling, tasting and adjustment. *Nukabot* senses environmental and biochemical conditions and produces conversational prompts or vocal expressions that invite a carer to respond. It does not merely display microbial data; it locates computation inside a culturally familiar, ongoing practice of reciprocal maintenance.
works.publics_text: Iterations have appeared in design, media-art and science venues in Japan, including Triennale-related, 21_21 DESIGN SIGHT and Miraikan contexts, alongside academic demonstrations (**D/CR; verify venue-year pairing before publication**). Participating publics include researchers, designers, fermenters and household carers. Museum visitors are encountered publics. Microbial communities are living participants whose conditions are sensed, but humans author the interface and consume its products.
works.rq1: Microbial activity is invisible and care knowledge is sensory, tacit and temporally distributed. A one-off exhibit struggles to convey this duration.
works.rq2: The work uses a familiar vessel, chemical/environmental sensing, conversational voice, humour and repeated care routines. Cultural familiarity bridges expert microbiology and domestic practice.
works.rq3: Voice can sustain attention but implies an integrated microbial speaker where a multispecies community and technical model exist. Sensor values may displace embodied knowledge even as the project celebrates it. The microbes’ flourishing remains entangled with human taste, food production and eventual consumption.
works.evaluation: A valuable long-duration care case if voice and metabolism are kept analytically separate.
works.configuration: Invisible microbial transformation → situated sensing and conversational care → household/design/museum publics → documented prototypes and exhibitions → ventriloquism, cultural-translation and instrumental-care tensions → make model limits and human–microbial reciprocity explicit.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for concept and prototype; presentation chronology and public-response claims require final cross-check against each credited iteration. Sources: [ACM Digital Library record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3313831.3376630) and [`portfolio/nukabot.md`](../../portfolio/nukabot.md).
works.format: sensorised fermentation vessel with voice interface

short.rq1: Microbial fermentation is invisible and care knowledge is difficult to carry into digital public culture.
short.rq2: Sensors, conversational personification, culturally familiar vessel and long museum deployments.
short.rq3: The microbial voice is designer-written; cultural heritage, maintenance labour and organismal welfare can be obscured by cuteness.

works.title: The Great Animal Orchestra
works.creators: Bernie Krause and United Visual Artists
works.occasions: Fondation Cartier; Peabody Essex Museum; Exploratorium; international tour
works.publics: Ticketed museum visitors, sound-art/science publics; recorded ecosystems represented
works.summary:
*The Great Animal Orchestra* is an immersive installation developed by bioacoustician Bernie Krause with United Visual Artists. It was commissioned by Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain in 2016 from Krause’s long-term archive of habitat recordings.

Panoramic spectrograms move in synchrony with multichannel soundscapes recorded across habitats. Visitors hear biophony as patterned ecological organisation and can visually follow acoustic niches, absences and transformations. The installation makes a scientific archive sensorially navigable while framing soundscape loss as evidence of environmental change.
works.publics_text: First presented at Fondation Cartier in Paris in 2016, the installation has toured and entered museum and science-centre contexts, including the Peabody Essex Museum and Exploratorium (**D**). Encountered publics include art, natural-history, science-centre and educational audiences. Krause and institutional teams are participating publics; recorded animal communities and habitats are represented participants, not live ones. Conservation institutions are potential decision-capable publics.
works.rq1: Ecological degradation can occur acoustically before it becomes visually obvious, while distant habitats remain outside most people’s experience. A specialist archive does not automatically become a public encounter.
works.rq2: Tactics include long-term field recording, an archive spanning locations and decades, multichannel immersion, synchronised spectrograms, narrative comparison and international touring.
works.rq3: A beautiful museum environment can make disappearance intensely felt, yet also aestheticise it. Curatorial selection gives coherence to disparate habitats and may obscure Indigenous territories, local conflicts and recording conditions. Attendance evidences exposure rather than conservation action.
works.evaluation: A major public bridge between scientific archive and affect, not a demonstrated conservation intervention.
works.configuration: Remote and vanishing biophony → archive plus audiovisual immersion → international museum/science public → documented touring and repeat presentation → aestheticisation, territorial context and action-gap tensions → attach each soundscape to situated ecological and governance histories.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for artistic form and exhibition history; limited public-outcome and conservation-impact evaluation. Sources: [Fondation Cartier project page](https://www.fondationcartier.com/en/exhibitions/the-great-animal-orchestra) and [`portfolio/great-animal-orchestra.md`](../../portfolio/great-animal-orchestra.md).

short.rq1: Long-term habitat sound loss is dispersed across remote places and expert archives.
short.rq2: Field-recording archive, spectrogram-light translation, reflective architecture and international touring.
short.rq3: Museum beauty can turn disappearance into contemplative spectacle; access is ticketed and action outcomes are unknown.

works.title: Ghost Forest
works.creators: Maya Lin; Madison Square Park Conservancy
works.entity: Dead Atlantic white cedars and climate-stressed forests
works.occasions: Madison Square Park, New York, May–November 2021
works.publics: Park passers-by, art/climate publics, local organisations; source forests implicated
works.summary:
*Ghost Forest* was a public installation by Maya Lin presented by Madison Square Park Conservancy in New York from May to November 2021. It comprised forty-nine Atlantic white cedar trees killed by saltwater intrusion and sourced from New Jersey’s Pine Barrens.

The standing dead trees abruptly changed a familiar urban park into an image of forest loss. Sound components and related public programmes connected the installation to threatened habitats, climate change and local ecological action. Because the trees were materially present rather than represented by images, visitors encountered both monumentality and decay over months.
works.publics_text: The principal site was Madison Square Park, a free civic space traversed by commuters, residents, tourists, school groups and art audiences (**D**). Forestry and conservation partners, educators and park staff were participating publics. The source forest and communities affected by coastal change constitute affected publics. City, park and climate organisations are potential decision-capable publics. The dead cedars are material witnesses, not living collaborators.
works.rq1: Forest die-off is geographically distributed and can remain abstract to city publics. Climate causality is difficult to infer from an individual dead tree without contextual explanation.
works.rq2: Tactics include material relocation, monumental repetition, free civic siting, duration, sound, education and public programming.
works.rq3: Moving dead trees produces a forceful public witness but detaches them from the source ecosystem. Monumental spectacle can individualise “climate change” while saltwater intrusion, land management and environmental inequality require specific accounts. Transport, installation and post-exhibition material afterlife are part of the work’s politics.
works.evaluation: A powerful material witness with a clearer civic pathway than most climate spectacles.
works.configuration: Distant distributed forest death → relocated cedar monument in a daily urban route → broad civic public → sustained exposure and programme participation → displacement, carbon/logistics and causal-simplification tensions → document sourcing, afterlife and locally actionable climate relations.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for dates, material composition and programming; limited for longitudinal public action. Sources: [Madison Square Park Conservancy project page](https://madisonsquarepark.org/art/exhibitions/maya-lin-ghost-forest/) and [`portfolio/ghost-forest.md`](../../portfolio/ghost-forest.md).

sources.label: Madison Square Park Conservancy project page

works.entity_short: dead Atlantic white cedars and climate-stressed forests
works.format: public-park installation with sound and planting programme

short.rq1: Saltwater intrusion and forest death are geographically diffuse and easy for urban publics to ignore.
short.rq2: Relocation of actual dead trees, free civic siting, vanished-species soundscape and companion planting.

works.title: Particle Falls
works.creators: Andrea Polli with Chuck Varga
works.occasions: ZERO1/01SJ 2010; Philadelphia Sensing Change; later redeployments
works.publics: Street passers-by, residents, arts/science publics, pollution-affected communities
works.summary:
*Particle Falls* is a public artwork by Andrea Polli and Chuck Varga, first realised in 2010. It uses a nephelometer or comparable air-quality sensor to convert changing particulate levels into a large real-time projection on an urban façade.

The projection resembles a luminous waterfall. When airborne particulate concentration rises, visual disruptions appear in the falling field. Passing traffic and local conditions therefore become immediately associated with a changing public image. The work transforms ambient exposure from a numerical report into a shared street event.
works.publics_text: Documented installations include San Jose during the 2010 ZERO1 context and Philadelphia in 2013, with later versions in other cities (**D/secondary**). Encountered publics include pedestrians, commuters, residents and festival visitors. People living or working near the sensor are affected publics, while public-health departments, transport planners and municipal officials are decision-capable publics. Air and particulate matter are sensed material actors.
works.rq1: Particulate pollution is invisible in ordinary experience and often encountered through delayed regional statistics that obscure local peaks and unequal exposure.
works.rq2: Tactics include real-time sensing, monumental public projection, intuitive visual change, street-level placement and a direct link between local activity and display.
works.rq3: A single sensor produces a highly local account whose calibration and siting matter. Visibility may create concern without identifying responsibility or enabling action. The aesthetically attractive waterfall can make pollution watchable while communities continue to bear exposure.
works.evaluation: A strong civic-sensing bridge with plausible immediacy but little evidence of policy effect.
works.configuration: Invisible local particulate exposure → live façade visualisation → street and environmental-health public → documented urban installations → sensor-siting, aestheticisation and action-gap tensions → publish measurement limits and connect display to health and transport decisions.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for public form and real-time translation; limited for behavioural, public-health or policy outcomes. Sources: [Andrea Polli’s project page](https://andreapolli.com/particle-falls/) and [`portfolio/particle-falls.md`](../../portfolio/particle-falls.md).

short.rq1: Air pollution is ambient, invisible and unevenly experienced.
short.rq2: Nephelometer data, fifteen-second visual updates, free public facade and redeployable web data.
short.rq3: Aesthetic visibility may substitute for exposure reduction; sensor placement and whose air counts remain political.

works.title: Squeeker: The Mouse Coach
works.creators: Jiabao Li
works.occasions: IDFA DocLab 2023; Ars Electronica 2024; TEI 2026
works.publics: Festival/app publics, runners, lab-animal issue publics; live mouse affected
works.summary:
*Squeeker: The Mouse Coach* is a 2023–present project by Jiabao Li and collaborators. It combines a live mouse, an exercise wheel, a mobile running interface, documentary media and later research framing; versions were shown at IDFA DocLab in 2023, Ars Electronica in 2024 and an ACM TEI context in 2026.

A human runner follows exercise prompts linked to a mouse’s wheel activity, reversing the familiar laboratory arrangement in which mice perform for human observation. The mouse becomes a charismatic “coach,” and humour makes experimental power relations easy to grasp. App and film components extend the encounter beyond the live apparatus.
works.publics_text: Documented contexts span immersive-documentary, media-art and research venues (**D**). Encountered publics include festival visitors, app users, runners, designers and animal–computer interaction researchers. Participating publics include the mouse, handlers, the production team and human runners. Animal-care personnel and venue ethics structures are decision-capable for the live animal, while laboratory institutions form the wider issue public.
works.rq1: Laboratory animals’ repetitive labour and asymmetrical relation to research systems usually remain hidden. Animal experimentation is also polarised in public discourse, making sustained reflection difficult.
works.rq2: The work uses role reversal, humour, cross-species synchronisation, bodily exercise, a charismatic individual animal, documentary narrative and distribution across app, film and installation.
works.rq3: Calling the mouse a coach symbolically redistributes authority, but the human team still designs the enclosure, interprets the activity and controls circulation. A visible live animal generates ethical immediacy while also becoming an exhibition apparatus. Publicly available project records do not by themselves establish a complete welfare protocol or the mouse’s freedom to disengage.
works.evaluation: Provocative but ethically high-risk; retain as a critical case, not a success exemplar.
works.configuration: Hidden laboratory hierarchy → comic mouse–human role reversal → festival, running and ACI publics → documented presentations and interactions → symbolic-agency, welfare and apparatus tensions → publish care, rest, withdrawal and decision protocols alongside the work.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong for concept and presentation trajectory; welfare conditions and audience consequences need project-team or venue documentation before stronger claims. Sources: [Jiabao Li project page](https://www.jiabaoli.org/squeeker) and [`portfolio/squeeker.md`](../../portfolio/squeeker.md).

short.rq1: Laboratory-animal hierarchy is socially normalised and difficult to question beyond specialist ethics debates.
short.rq2: Role reversal, absurd humour, app notifications, exercise target and multi-format circulation.
short.rq3: The mouse remains an apparatus; no checked welfare protocol or consent mechanism supports the empowered-mouse framing.

works.title: The Elephant in the Room
works.creators: Jiabao Li with legal, NGO, performance and media collaborators
works.entity: Captive Asian elephants and animal entertainment
works.medium: AR; interactive 3D; drone sound; music video; campaign
works.occasions: Online campaign; 28 March 2024 appellate hearing context; press circulation
