works.evaluation: One of the strongest complete RQ1-RQ3 cases because provocation develops into accountable infrastructure proposals.
works.configuration: Hidden microbial labour and protocol-defined error → revolt provocation plus counter-useful toolmaking → biologist, designer, bioart and HCI publics → substantial workshop/interview evidence → anthropomorphism, safety and governance tensions → preserve revolt as a heuristic and pursue validated, accountable infrastructure changes.
works.evidence_boundary: One of the portfolio’s strongest peer-reviewed method cases: 28 workshop participants, 24 artefacts and 16 interviews. Proposed sterilisation, mixed-culture and governance adaptations were not technically validated, and no microbial preference or welfare was established. Sources: [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3641981), [`references/chen2024microbial.md`](../chen2024microbial.md) and [`research/.../mthd-0040...md`](../../research/more-than-human-design-review/knowledge/papers/mthd-0040-2024-microbial-revolt-redefining-biolab-tools-and-practices-for-more-than-human-care-ecologies.md).
works.entity_short: laboratory microbes, tools, waste streams and regulators
works.format: three workshops, Microbial Chindogu and follow-up interviews

short.rq1: Laboratory tools and protocols hide microbial time, labour, death, escape, contamination and possible nonparticipation.
short.rq2: Feral/lab comparison, revolt lens, 24 deliberately human-useless Chindogu tools, disciplinary comparison and infrastructure proposals.
short.rq3: Revolt is an anthropomorphic thinking tool, not microbial-intention evidence; openness, mixed cultures and wild sampling also create biosafety and environmental risks.

works.title: Labour Provenance
works.creators: Yuning Chen, Elise Cachat, Larissa Pschetz
works.entity: Distributed organisms behind biodesign supply chains
works.occasions: Five-month lab case and four-group workshop; CHI 2025, Yokohama
works.publics: Lab collaborators, workshop practitioners, CHI/biodesign publics; focal and “shadow” organisms implicated
works.summary:
*Labour Provenance* is a 2024–2025 project and CHI 2025 paper by Yuning Chen, Elise Cachat and Larissa Pschetz. It develops an analytic framework from a five-month experiment attempting to hybridise human and yeast cells and from a reflexive workshop with biodesign practitioners.

The authors deconstruct a six-step biological protocol and trace the living origins behind cell lines, genes, enzymes, media, markers and industrial reagents. A nominally two-organism experiment expands into a distributed ecology involving bacteria, viruses, fungi, plants, livestock, marine organisms, agriculture and manufacturing. The framework distinguishes metabolic, resistance and sustenance labour, five structural job positions and degrees of subsumption into production.
works.publics_text: The research setting included the university synthetic-biology laboratory, collaborators and a workshop organised in four groups around participants’ own biological projects (**D**). The paper was presented at CHI 2025 in Yokohama and received an Honourable Mention (**D**). Participating publics include the authors, laboratory collaborators and workshop practitioners; encountered publics include HCI, STS, biodesign and synthetic-biology communities. Suppliers, agricultural industries and research institutions are decision-capable publics. The many focal and “shadow” organisms are materially implicated but not directly consulted.
works.rq1: Barcodes, standard reagents and protocols erase living origins. Focal organisms receive attention while the metabolic, resistance and sustenance work of organisms across supply chains remains structurally invisible.
works.rq2: Tactics include stepwise protocol deconstruction, centre-to-periphery provenance mapping, labour categories, job-position analysis, degrees of subsumption, a practitioner workshop and an audit of sustainability claims across living inputs.
works.rq3: Labour language reveals extraction and control, but can again define organisms by productivity. Provenance remains incomplete where suppliers use proprietary or generic labels. Workshop participants also showed charisma bias, recognising mammalian harm more readily than bacterial exploitation. Symbolic acknowledgement can coexist with unchanged material extraction.
works.evaluation: The portfolio's strongest analytic counterweight to spectacular empathy and first-person umwelt simulation.
works.configuration: Standardised invisibility of distributed living work → protocol audit and labour-provenance map → laboratory, workshop, HCI and supply-chain publics → rich case/framework evidence → productive-role reduction, incomplete traceability and unequal concern → use as the portfolio’s analytic counterweight to spectacular empathy.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong peer-reviewed case and method evidence; framework categories prompt analysis rather than provide a complete lifecycle audit or validated welfare measure. Sources: [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713272), [`references/chen2025labour.md`](../chen2025labour.md) and [`research/.../mthd-0068...md`](../../research/more-than-human-design-review/knowledge/papers/mthd-0068-2025-labour-provenance-as-a-lens-to-reveal-more-than-human-ecologies-in-biological-design-and-hci.md).
works.entity_short: distributed organisms and supply ecologies behind biodesign
works.format: protocol deconstruction, provenance map and reflexive workshop

short.rq1: Standardised reagents and protocols erase living origins and distributed metabolic, resistance and sustenance labour.
short.rq2: Stepwise protocol audit, centre-to-periphery provenance map, labour categories, five job positions, subsumption analysis and practitioner workshop.
short.rq3: Labour language exposes exploitation but can again value organisms through productivity; provenance is incomplete and concern remains charisma-biased.

works.title: Morality Calculus / Food Theatre / Chewing It Over
works.creators: Yuning Chen with Elise Cachat, Adam Frank, Larissa Pschetz and collaborators
works.entity: Human–microbe hybrid fictions, fermentation microbes and shadow organisms
works.medium: Bioart installation; seven-session public dining theatre
works.occasions: Summerhall/Edinburgh Science Festival 2024; CHI 2026
works.publics: Free exhibition visitors, 47 dining participants, facilitators/researchers; microbes and donor organisms represented
works.summary:
This connected 2024–2026 project trajectory is led by Yuning Chen. *Morality Calculus* was developed with Elise Cachat and other scientific/artistic collaborators; its public Food Theatre informed the 2026 CHI paper *Chewing It Over* by Yuning Chen, Adam Frank and Larissa Pschetz. The installation and performance are treated as one case with two public phases rather than inflated into separate portfolio items.

The installation presents bread associated with a human–yeast cell hybrid experiment, fluorescent crumbs, cell-like blocks and evidence of organisms whose genes, enzymes or sera supported the work. The Food Theatre turns the question into an embodied public event: participants choose, discuss and eat vegetarian/vegan fermented foods given fictional human–microbe hybrid histories involving compression, auxotrophy, sterilisation, heat shock, isolation or bioremediation. Scales, magnets and “moral allergens” make the desire to quantify worth visibly incoherent.
works.publics_text: *Morality Calculus* was shown free at Summerhall’s War Memorial Gallery as part of Edinburgh Science Festival 2024, presented with ASCUS Art & Science and institutional partners (**D**). Seven two-hour lunchtime dining sessions involved 47 participants across ages, ethnicities and professions (**D**). Written notes, audio and opt-in visual records supported the 2026 CHI analysis. Free exhibition visitors are encountered publics; the 47 diners, hosts and researchers are participating publics. Synthetic-biology institutions and ethics bodies are decision-capable. Actual fermented microbes were present in food, while the human–microbial hybrids and suffering histories served as fictional proxies.
works.rq1: Mechanistic parts language hides microbial labour and “shadow organisms.” Ready-made ethics based on consumer safety, cannibalism taboo, paid human consent or causal distance can close inquiry before nonhuman relations are considered.
works.rq2: Tactics include material provenance display, hybrid-bread provocation, public dining, ingestion, fictional organism biographies grounded in real stresses, scientific staging, moral weights, disgust, corporal compassion and facilitation that values hesitation over consensus.
works.rq3: Bodily analogy can reveal shared vulnerability but may appropriate histories of refugees, disability, labour exploitation, racial violence or other human suffering to give microbes emotional weight. Human consent can become a moral pass while microbial nonparticipation remains unaddressed. Consumer risk may recentre the diner. Affect, disgust or empathy cannot be treated as a linear measure of ethical improvement.
works.evaluation: A mature public RQ3 case because it keeps contradiction and moral hesitation visible rather than claiming consensus.
works.configuration: Hidden microbial labour and premature moral closure → provenance installation plus consequential dining theatre → free festival visitors and 47 participating diners → strong qualitative evidence of disagreement and hesitation → proxy, appropriation, consent and commensurability tensions → treat moral hesitation as political capacity, not a quantified attitude outcome.
works.evidence_boundary: Strong peer-reviewed public-method evidence: seven sessions and 47 participants. Group talk was difficult to capture, session procedures changed after the first two groups, magnet counts are not quantitative data, the hybrid foods were fictional and no behavioural follow-up or microbial outcome was measured. Sources: [Edinburgh Science Festival/ASCUS exhibition record](https://www.ascus.org.uk/whats-on/earthsoilfilth-exhibition-esf2024-da9ep), [CHI 2026 DOI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791048), [`references/chen2026chewing.md`](../chen2026chewing.md) and [`research/.../mthd-0079...md`](../../research/more-than-human-design-review/knowledge/papers/mthd-0079-2026-chewing-it-over-revealing-tensions-and-new-directions-for-more-than-human-relational-ethics-through-.md).
works.entity_short: human-microbe hybrid fictions, fermentation microbes and shadow organisms
works.format: bioart installation plus seven-session public dining theatre

short.rq1: Microbial alterity and labour are obscured by mechanistic parts language and ready-made ethics that rapidly close discussion.
short.rq2: Hybrid bread installation, provenance display, fictional foods, eating, moral weights, disgust and facilitated hesitation across seven sessions with 47 participants.
short.rq3: Human consent, consumer safety and analogies to vulnerable human groups can recenter humans; fictional proxies and affect do not demonstrate microbial welfare or ethical improvement.
